text: Artifact creatures, Spacecraft, counters and eight-power attackers. The reviewers found white the least exciting colour at common and uncommon, with the most commons in the D range, but loved its rares: the white mythics are close to the best cards in the set. Each white pair stands on a different plan, so white cards rarely fit all four decks.
Draftsim's best white commons are the exiling artifact, the Doctor that adds a counter or draws, and the two-mana ship.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): white has the lowest-rated commons, and three of its four pairs are below average. RW is the exception.

Spacecraft, dilemmas, bounce and card draw. The reviewers rated blue possibly the best colour at common, thanks to all its card draw, and among the worst at uncommon and rare. The uncommons are flat, nearly all graded between D+ and B-, with one standout: the expensive Strange New Worlds spell that draws and makes two bodies.

Blue's removal taps, stuns, bounces or puts a creature on top of the library; none of it kills. Hard counters are better than usual here. Draftsim's best blue commons are the bouncing artifact creature, the ship that draws and the instant that tucks an attacker.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): blue's commons sit in the middle; UR and GU do well, UB worst of all.

Klingons, Borg, dilemmas and the graveyard. The reviewers called black middle of the road in power, but every deck has something in black, so it gets fought over. It has the cleanest removal: an unconditional instant at common, a cheap -2/-2 that grows when you sacrifice, and a two-mana kill spell at uncommon.
Draftsim's best black commons are the instant kill spell, the -2/-2 and the sticky Borg creature. Many black uncommons are dilemma payoffs, which the reviewers rated low.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): black's uncommons are the weakest group; BR and BG are near the top, WB and UB near the bottom.

Klingons, landfall and eight-power attackers. The reviewers rated red's commons possibly the worst in the set, though not bad, all in a flat power band, with three common removal spells at one, three and five mana. The uncommons are better, with several B grades, and the X-damage instant is the pick of them.
Draftsim's best red commons are the one-mana burn spell, the pinging Romulan and the beam me up token maker.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): red's commons and uncommons are winning the most of any colour, and drafters still let them go late. If that lasts, red is underrated.

Landfall, Strange New Worlds, counters and self-mill. The reviewers called green's commons various shades of C, few of them wasted, and gave green the highest density of very powerful rares. Half its commons feed the slow GU and BG decks, the other half the RG and GW attackers.

Draftsim's best green commons are the land-milling creature, the two-drop that taps for any colour and the bite spell. The six-drop that returns a card and makes 3/3s is the best green uncommon by both Draftsim and the data.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): green's rares are the best in the set, and RG and BG are two of the three best decks.

archetypes.name: Spacecraft tempo

text: Tempo and enters-the-battlefield value, leaning on a few Spacecraft. The signpost protects your ships and loots whenever it taps, which stationing does. Draftsim calls it Engineers and Spacecraft.
Both reviewers warn against overloading: two or three good ships, not five to ten. Each needs creatures to tap, and a deck with too many taps its blockers for nothing.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): below average, held back by white's commons.

key: Loots every time it taps to station. Spacecraft get hexproof on your turn.
Locks down a creature for two turns or makes two Clues.
Kills a tapped creature on entry, then becomes a flyer.

archetypes.name: Dilemmas

text: Modal spells and creatures (any card that says choose one counts as facing a dilemma) with payoffs that draw, drain or grow when you choose. The set has plenty of enablers, especially in black, and the reviewers think eight or nine is easy to reach.
The payoffs are thin by design. The reviewers' advice: play the good modal cards for what they do, use the blue payoff as a bonus, and don't go all in. Artifacts matter a little here too.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): the lowest deck win rate in the format so far.

key: The dilemma payoff: a card for every choice.
Cheap hybrid body with a modal enter trigger.

archetypes.name: Klingon aggro

text: Klingons, hasty 2/1 tokens and sacrifice. The reviewers describe it as doing a little more each turn rather than pure aggro: tokens that die anyway get turned into value, and menace plays well with the few tricks.
Most of the set's Klingons are here, so the Klingon trick and the card-drawing gold rare work. Red's burn and black's kill spells make it the pair with the most removal.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): second best by deck win rate, and its gold cards are among the best.

key: A hybrid two-drop that leaves a hasty token behind. The best gold uncommon.
A hasty attacker every turn, plus a sacrifice outlet.
Grows when anything dies and draws off sacrificed Klingons.

archetypes.name: Landfall stompy

text: Landfall stompy: as many stats on the board as fast as possible, with landfall triggers on the way. The reviewers note slightly weaker commons but nice uncommons, and expect it to be competitive if the format leaves room for aggression.
Landfall creatures are weak as late draws, so play them on curve while land drops remain. Extra land drops, instant-speed Planet tokens and land searchers give second triggers in a turn.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): the best deck so far.

theme.label: landfall
enabler: basic land card or Planet card

key: Ramps on every land drop and turns spare lands into cards.
Haste for the team and a land off the top.
A 2/2 token on every land drop.

archetypes.name: Doctors and counters

text: +1/+1 counters and a wide board, with payoffs that draw cards or spread more counters. The sealed guide calls it a classic limited theme, and the reviewers like that it works with Spacecraft, whose charge counters count.
The engines are good even if the creature only connects a couple of times. Draftsim calls it the Doctors deck.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): below average, and both gold counter payoffs are losing so far. Watch them.

key: Draws whenever a creature with a counter connects.

archetypes.name: Borg artifacts

text: Borg: artifact creatures and lords that pump them, mostly aggressive but able to grind. The sealed guide calls it a pretty strong deck with a lot of strong cards, and the reviewers expect it to be one of the best. It was one of the two most played decks on Arena in the first days.
It wants a lot of artifact creatures, around 14 or 15 in a 17-creature deck by the reviewers' count, because several cards buff all of them. The double-strike rare is the top end.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): below average so far; the commons that fill the deck are underperforming.

key: Lord for artifact creatures, or a removal spell from your hand.
Hybrid lifelinker that taxes their best card.
Double strike for every artifact creature.

archetypes.name: Scientists and spells

text: Cheap creatures, instants and sorceries, and payoffs that care about noncreature spells. Draftsim calls it Scientists. Little flying and reach in the set means evasive creatures get in, and red's burn pushes the last points through.
The signpost two-drop wants about ten noncreature spells; eight is playable, fewer is not.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): above average, and the signpost is one of the best gold cards.

key: Finds a spell from the top four. A top uncommon.
Copies a creature each turn you cast a spell. Weaker than it looks.

archetypes.name: Graveyard value

text: Mill, surveil and bring things back, with payoffs that trigger when a card leaves your graveyard. The reviewers point out several commons mill and then return a card, which makes leaves-the-graveyard triggers easy, and milled beam me up cards are free spells.
A grindy deck: make good trades, avoid racing and let the value creatures and black removal take over.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): third best, and BG cards win more here than in other pairs.

key: A two-drop that levels into a 3/4 that surveils.
Surveils every turn and draws when a card leaves the graveyard.
Brings back a creature card, then recycles itself.

archetypes.name: Command crew

text: Play a creature every turn and attack with eight or more total power to switch on the payoffs. The reviewers found it hard to judge: eight is easy to reach (a two-drop, a three-drop and a four-drop), but trades drop you back below it, tricks play poorly and equipment adds power to one creature only.
Draftsim calls it Command crew. Officer tokens and cheap high-power creatures help, and the common three-drop that pumps an attacker each turn is a key card.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): fourth best, and that three-drop is the best common so far.

key: Card advantage on every attack with eight power.
Hybrid two-drop that doubles its power.
The best common in the set. Gives menace once you reach eight power.

archetypes.name: Strange New Worlds

text: Count differently named lands: Planet duals at common, shock lands at rare, the colourless Anomaly lands and New Planet tokens. The reviewers rate the support as deep and the payoffs as strong, and it was one of the two most played decks on Arena in the first days.

A two-colour deck with a dual and a colourless land reaches about three names, the floor; mid-game GU decks reach four to seven. Draft fixing highly here. The sealed guide adds a mill plan with the blue card that takes their top land.
Early 17Lands numbers (first four days, too soon to trust): just below the middle.

key: Power equals your land names. A top gold uncommon.
Two bodies and two cards, cheaper with each land name.
The GU Planet dual. The best of the common lands.

text: Star Trek is a Universes Beyond set with crews, starships and planets. Each two-colour pair has its own plan, from Klingon aggro to counting differently named lands. Most decks play cheap creatures with enter-the-battlefield effects, and beam me up lets you cast cards again from the graveyard by picking one of those creatures back up.

This guide starts from Draftsim's set review and rankings and adds what two podcast hosts said in a seven-part set review and a sealed guide. The 17Lands numbers on the card pages are from the first four days only, so they show up as early hints, not verdicts. The guide will be redone once there is real data. Where it says strong players, it means 17Lands users who win 60% or more of their games.

sections.heading: The format in short
list: A deep, flat format: few bombs, few unplayables, and the reviewers expect every pair to be viable. Filler matters more than usual because packs have fewer standout cards.
Lots of cheap creatures with enter effects, so curves are low and beam me up is the defining mechanic. Pick up a one- or two-drop to recast a spell, never your five-drop.
Removal is narrower than usual: damage, size limits, sorcery speed. Take the clean answers when you see them.
Spacecraft are good in twos and threes, not tens. They need creatures to tap, and they carry most of the set's flying.
Synergy over raw power: build toward your pair's plan, but don't go all in on the themes with thin payoffs (dilemmas above all). The Mission enchantments are a trap everyone agrees on.
Good mana matters. Take two Planet duals for your colours; GU wants as many lands with different names as it can get.
Early data hint: red and green are winning the most and UB the least. Too soon to draft by, worth watching.

text: Early picks: power first, then removal. The green, white and red rares at the top of the set come first whatever their colour, then clean removal (red burn, black kill spells, the green bite spell), then the best gold uncommons. A strong gold two-drop is a fine early pick, but it ties you to two colours on pick one.

sections.heading: Colours
text: The reviewers expect no colour to dominate: green has the most powerful rares, white the best mythics, blue the deepest commons, red flat commons and better uncommons, black something for every deck. Early data so far favour red and green, and red commons are going late. If good red keeps coming in pack 1, it is probably open.

sections.heading: Which themes are worth it
text: Some plans have plenty of payoffs and some have few, and the reviewers flag the thin ones. Land names (GU), Klingons (BR), landfall (RG) and the graveyard (BG) have real payoffs at common and uncommon. Dilemmas (UB) have many enablers and few rewards; the reviewers' advice is not to go all in. Early data also have the GW counters payoffs and WB's Borg commons behind.
In practice: draft good cards and removal, and let the theme decide close picks. Take a payoff early only when you already hold its support.
Sharing a mechanic isn't support. A card that rewards you for land names needs real land names; a card that rewards Klingons needs Klingons.

sections.heading: Lands
text: The common Planet duals (tapped, gain one life, two colours) win about as often as an average card and still go late. In a normal two-colour deck take two of yours: better mana without too many slow turns. In GU take every one you can, because each one is another land name.
The colourless Anomaly lands that sacrifice for an effect are a real cost to your coloured mana. Play one at most. The rare shock lands are fine but not worth a high pick outside GU.

sections.heading: Main colour and second colour
text: This held in Bloomburrow's draft data and is general enough to carry over; TRK's draft data isn't public yet. You don't draft two colours at once. Pack 1 settles one colour, and the second gets decided in pack 2 once you see what the table is leaving alone.

Count as you go. A finished deck is about 13 cards of the main colour and 8 of the second. Once the main colour has about seven good cards, another average one only pushes out your weakest. A decent card in the colour you are short of adds one.

sections.heading: Reading what is open
text: In packs 1 and 3 the same neighbour passes to you; in pack 2 it is the other one. So what you see late in pack 1 tells you about pack 3. A signal is a good card arriving later than it normally gets taken. In this set, the late red commons are a signal only if they are later than usual, because everyone is passing them a bit.

sections.heading: Where people go wrong
text: Flashy rares with weak results get taken in the first three picks (see Traps). The dilemma payoffs, the Mission enchantments and the counters gold cards look like build-arounds and play like filler. The Sleepers page lists cards that win more than their pick order suggests.

17Lands hasn't published TRK's game data yet, so this page can't give the measured deck numbers the Bloomburrow guide has (land count, creature count, curve by result). What follows is the reviewers' advice plus what the card data already show. Expect this page to change.

sections.heading: The shape
list: Two colours. There are no over-the-top bombs worth bending the mana for, so splash only a strong single-pip rare or removal spell, and only with a dual or a green fixer.
Keep the curve low and affect the board early. Both reviewers expect pressure from cheap creatures, more than in the last set, and a good one-drop is worth more than usual.
Plenty of creatures. Spacecraft, beam me up and the eight-power cards all need bodies.
Two or three Spacecraft at most, and only the good ones.
Count beam me up cards as half a card more: you will cast the good ones twice. Pick up cheap creatures to do it.

sections.heading: Lands
text: The reviewers build with 17 lands. Take two Planet duals for your colours in a normal deck; GU can play four to seven. Play at most one colourless Anomaly land, ideally as a seventeenth or eighteenth land when you can't cut a basic.
Land cyclers are weaker here than in recent sets: the bodies are big but plain, and there is little to reanimate them with.

sections.heading: Removal
text: Removal in this set is mostly damage, a size condition or sorcery speed, so plan what each spell can kill. Black's -X/-X and the four-power condition on the white common both have awkward gaps. Take a solid removal spell over a pretty good creature: the reviewers felt the shortage, and the data back them, since nearly all the clean removal wins above average.

sections.heading: Cards to leave out
text: The Mission enchantments are too slow for what they give. Both reviewers said so and all of them lose in the data. The Test sorceries and instants are mostly weak too; the least bad is red's Klingon one, in BR. Stun and tap removal is worse than it looks against beam me up decks, which happily pick the stunned creature back up.

Bloomburrow was about tribes, and the last set was balanced enough that every pair worked. This one is about value and second chances: cheap creatures that do something when they enter, ways to cast spells twice, and a mechanic for each pair that asks you to build a certain way.

sections.heading: Beam me up and enter effects
text: The reviewers expect beam me up to define the set. You cast the card again from your graveyard by returning a creature you control to your hand, which is a cost unless the creature does something when it enters. In this set many do, so a cheap creature with a good enter effect is worth more than usual, and stun or tap removal is worse, because the opponent just picks the creature up and replays it.

sections.heading: A plan for every pair, some thin
text: Every pair has its own mechanic: land names, landfall, eight power, Klingons, Borg artifacts, counters, dilemmas, spells, the graveyard and Spacecraft. The reviewers' warning is that several have plenty of enablers and few payoffs, so you build toward the plan without needing it. Dilemmas are the clearest case: many cards trigger them, very few reward you.

sections.heading: Flat power, deep packs
text: There are fewer standout cards per pack than in the last set and few true bombs, but also few unplayables; the reviewers handed out hardly any F grades. Packs fill up with cards that look like filler and play better than they look. Removal is specific (size, timing, damage), so it runs out and awkward spots come up.

sections.heading: Lands are a real pick
text: Ten common Planet duals, colourless lands that sacrifice for an effect, and cards that make New Planet tokens or put extra lands onto the battlefield. They fix your mana, feed GU's land-name count and give RG second landfall triggers. Most decks want two duals; GU wants many more.

sections.heading: More rares than usual
text: As a Universes Beyond set it has the same commons as a normal set, about ten extra uncommons and twenty extra rares, so you see any one uncommon or rare less often. Green has the deepest rares and the white mythics are among the best cards in the set.

sections.heading: What the early data hint at
text: Four days of 17Lands data point the same way in a few places: red is winning more than its reviews, and the dilemma, GW counters and Borg payoffs are winning less. Too early to draft by, but worth watching.

Each pair has a plan and a set of payoffs. Below is what each build-around needs, from the reviewers, with the reviewers' grade first and early data second. Real deck data will show how much the support adds; for now, take a payoff when you already hold some of what it wants.

sections.heading: Payoffs the reviewers like
text: Graded B- or better by at least one reviewer, and winning well in the early data too.
cards: Needs about ten noncreature, nonland cards. Eight is playable.
Five or six land names is ideal.
Land names: duals, Anomaly lands, New Planet tokens.
A deck where cards leave the graveyard.
Klingons for the card draw and fodder to sacrifice.
Land drops still to come, so play it on curve.
Mill and return effects. One trigger a turn is enough.
Four or five creatures with enter or death effects to bring back.

sections.heading: Payoffs to be careful with
text: The reviewers were lukewarm on most of these, and the early data are worse. Several are the gold cards of the thinnest themes.
cards: Modal cards: seven to nine of them. Still about 50%.
Creatures with counters, or a Spacecraft. Under 49%.
Noncreature spells and a creature worth copying.
Eight power and about 20 creatures. Average at best.
Three to five copies. Even then, below average.

sections.heading: How to use this
list: A payoff whose support you already hold is worth taking early. One with nothing behind it is a late pick.
Count the support you actually hold. A land-name card wants real land names, a Klingon card wants Klingons.
Sharing a mechanic isn't support. Modal cards are good on their own; the dilemma payoffs are not.
This page will be redone with deck data once 17Lands publishes it.

text: This is not a tribal set like Bloomburrow, but Draftsim builds five pairs around a creature type: Klingons (BR), Borg (WB), Scientists (UR), Doctors (GW) and Officers (RW). Only Klingons and Borg have many cards that reward the type itself; for the other three the type is mostly a label for the deck's style. The counts below are cards of that type with play data.

sections.heading: The five crews
list: Klingons (BR): 5 black, 4 red, 4 gold, plus the hasty Klingon tokens many cards make. The Klingon trick and the card-drawing gold rare reward them directly.
Borg (WB): 7 black, 6 white, 1 gold. All artifact creatures, and the WB lords pump every artifact creature, not only Borg. Borg don't count for Federation.
Scientists (UR): 18, mostly green and blue with five gold. Nothing rewards Scientists as such; the UR deck is about noncreature spells.
Doctors (GW): 9, green and white. A couple of cards turn a creature into a Doctor; the GW deck is really about +1/+1 counters.
Officers (RW): 33 across every colour, including most of the captains, plus the 1/1 red Officer tokens. They matter as bodies for eight power and for stationing.

sections.heading: Other types
list: Humans (50), Vulcans, Androids and Romulans are flavour. Federation counts how many different types you have among non-Borg creatures, so it wants a mix, not a tribe.

sections.heading: Spacecraft and Planets
text: Two card types do work like small tribes. There are 14 Spacecraft, spread across every colour, and some cards search for them, protect them or charge them. The 10 Planets are the common duals, and some cards search for them alongside basics. See the Spacecraft and Planets pages.
Tips from the set review and sealed guide that change how games go. These are the reviewers' experience from early drafts, not measured.

sections.heading: Beam me up and the graveyard
list: Pick up your cheapest creature with a good enter effect, never your five-drop. It is sorcery speed, so it can't save a creature from removal.
Beam me up cards are good to mill or discard: a looting effect that bins one is close to a free card.
Tap and stun effects are weak against beam me up decks. They just pick the stunned creature up and replay it.
Keep a beam me up card or a land in hand against discard, so you choose what goes.

sections.heading: Spacecraft
list: Against a charged ship, tap or stun it at instant speed, or tap it on their upkeep before they can station.
A tapper on your side stops the opponent stationing for a turn.
Ships are artifacts, so artifact removal and the RW signpost's sacrifice ability answer them. Opponents load them less when you can do that.

sections.heading: Sagas with a bad last chapter
text: A few sagas give you something now and hurt you on chapter three (a creature comes back for them, or you lose a land). Remove the saga before then: sacrifice it to a card that wants a nonland permanent, or blink it. Count those outs before you play one.
cards: Exiles a creature, but it returns on chapter three.
Sacrifices a saga before its last chapter and pings.

sections.heading: Combat
list: Most creatures are on the ground, so a cheap deathtouch blocker holds off a lot of attacks.
Fight spells are worse than they look: your creature often can't attack that turn and trades down. Cast them when the opponent is tapped out.
Combat tricks are weak here because few decks race. Cards that keep making creatures beat cards that win one fight.
Landfall tokens that can't block don't defend you. Play those decks as midrange and plan your sixth and seventh land drops.

sections.heading: Specific cards
cards: Take the Officer token mode almost every time.
Mostly a draw-two. The kill mode gives them two tokens.
Aim to cast it at about five mana; discard a spare land or a beam me up card.
Don't pair lock-down auras with edicts: the opponent sacrifices the enchanted creature.
Its untap works at instant speed, so it is an on-board trick in combat.
The Anomaly lands work as instant-speed threats; the red one can replace a trick. Play one at most.

sections.heading: Quick Draft
text: Arena's bots draft their own colours. If the bots next to you share your pair, the synergy cards you want won't wheel; a pair they avoid wheels more.

pages.title: Beam me up
pages.summary: Cast the card again from your graveyard by also returning a creature you control to your hand
pages.verdict: Good with cheap enter-the-battlefield creatures. The best ones are spells you want twice.

text: Beam me up works like flashback with an extra cost: return a creature you control to its owner's hand. That is a downside unless the creature does something when it enters, and in this set many do. Pick up a one- or two-drop and replay it; never return the five-drop. It is sorcery speed, so it can't save a creature from removal. Milling or discarding these cards is free value, which is why the graveyard decks like them.
The reviewers expected it to define the format. The data mostly agree for the burn and token spells and disagree for the white ones.
cards: Three damage twice. The best beam me up card.
A hasty token now and another later.
Counters twice still isn't enough. One of the weakest commons.

pages.title: Spacecraft
pages.summary: Artifacts you charge by tapping creatures (station); at enough counters they become flying creatures
pages.verdict: Play two or three good ones. More than that and they stop working.

text: To station, tap another creature you control as a sorcery and put charge counters equal to its power on the Spacecraft. At the number on the card (often six) it becomes an artifact creature, and most fly. Thresholds are lower than in the last set with Spacecraft. Most of the set's flying is on these ships, so a charged one gets in.

They need a fair creature count. A deck full of ships taps its blockers for nothing. The ones that come with a body or an enter effect play best. Against a loaded ship, a tap or stun effect at instant speed is a big tempo swing.
cards: The best card in the set by win rate. Casts a free spell on entry and every attack.
A two-mana ship that fetches a land. Solid filler for white.
Stuns on entry, then asks a lot. Below average.

pages.title: Strange New Worlds
pages.summary: Gets cheaper or bigger with each differently named land you control
pages.verdict: GU's mechanic. Strong payoffs that need real land variety.

text: It counts land names, not colours or types: two copies of the same dual count once, but every basic type, Planet dual, shock land, Anomaly land and New Planet token adds one. A plain two-colour deck with one dual reaches three, which is the floor. GU decks with several duals reach four to seven by the mid game, and the payoffs get very good there.
cards: Grows with land names and lets you play lands off the top.
The best blue uncommon. Cast it for about five mana.
A repeatable tapper that is too slow for most decks.

pages.title: Dilemmas
pages.summary: You face a dilemma whenever you choose a mode for a spell or ability
pages.verdict: Lots of enablers, weak payoffs. Play modal cards for what they do.

text: Every choose-one card, and every ability that asks you to choose, counts as facing a dilemma. The set is full of them, so any deck faces a few. The payoffs are what make it a plan: cards that draw, drain, grow or return when you choose. They are mostly in blue and black.

Those payoffs are among the worst cards in the set so far, and UB, the dilemma pair, is the worst deck. The reviewers saw it coming and warned against going all in. Modal cards are good because both modes are often worth a card, not because of the payoffs.
cards: A soft counter or a stun and a card. One of the better blue commons.
The weakest card in the set.

pages.title: Landfall
pages.summary: Triggers whenever a land enters under your control
pages.verdict: RG's mechanic, and the best deck. Play landfall cards on curve.

text: Landfall cards trigger on every land drop, so they are strong early and weak as late top-decks. Extra land drops, instant-speed Planet tokens and the green cards that put lands onto the battlefield give a second trigger in a turn. Most payoffs are red and green.
cards: A two-drop that hits hard on land turns. Goes late for how good it is.
Card advantage off land drops, but slow. One of the weaker Missions.

pages.title: Eight power
pages.summary: Bonuses when you attack while your creatures have total power 8 or more
pages.verdict: RW's mechanic. Easier to reach than it sounds; trades take it away.

text: Attack with eight or more total power on your side of the table and these cards switch on: extra cards, double power, menace, can't-block effects. A two-drop, a three-drop and a four-drop usually get there. Trades and removal knock you back below, so the deck wants a creature every turn rather than tricks. The common red three-drop that uses it is a key card for the deck.
cards: The best common in the set.
Stops a blocker on every big attack.
Cheap but below average so far.

pages.title: Borg and artifact creatures
pages.summary: Lords and engines that reward a board of artifact creatures
pages.verdict: WB's plan. Strong rares; needs a lot of artifact creatures.

text: Many creatures in this set are artifacts, and the Borg are WB's version of a tribe. The payoffs pump, draw or copy across all your artifact creatures, so they need a board of them: the reviewers count 14 or 15 in a 17-creature deck. Borg don't count for Federation.
The rare payoffs are excellent, and the reviewers expect WB to be one of the best decks. Early data have its common and uncommon Borg underperforming, so lean on the rares and the gold cards.
cards: Double strike for the team. A bomb in the right deck.
Makes a Borg token on every hit.
Only as big as your artifact creature count. Weak.

pages.title: Federation
pages.summary: Counts the creature types among your non-Borg creatures
pages.verdict: Easy to misread. Only a few cards below rare.

text: Federation counts creature types, not creatures: a Human Officer counts two, and a second Human Officer adds nothing. Borg don't count. With the set's many types, four or five is normal by the mid game. It appears on only a handful of cards below rare.
cards: A rare that turns Federation into a big pump every turn.
Flash removal that is often too small. Below average.

pages.title: Missions
pages.summary: Uncommon enchantments that collect quest counters for a bigger effect
pages.verdict: A trap cycle. All of them lose.

text: Each Mission asks you to do something (cast noncreature spells, play creatures, have creatures die), gives a small effect each time and a bigger one at a set number of counters. They are too slow for what they give, and the reviewers, Draftsim and the data all agree. Three of them are among the ten weakest cards in the set.

pages.title: Planets and lands
pages.summary: Common tapped duals named after planets, New Planet tokens and land-searching cards
pages.verdict: Better than they look. Two in most decks, many more in GU.

text: The ten common Planets are tapped duals that gain a life. They win about average and still go late: the GU one is among the best commons in the set. Several cards make a New Planet token, a tapped land that taps for any colour, and the green land searchers can find Planets as well as basics. Every Planet is another land name for Strange New Worlds and another landfall trigger for RG.
cards: The GU dual. The best of the common lands.
The red Anomaly land: removal in your land slot.

text: The cards that take over a game, all rares and mythics. Most of them have only 500 to 1,300 games behind them so far, so the exact order will move. Green has the most.
cards: A free spell when it enters and on every attack. The best card in the set so far.
A wave of tokens, then counters whenever your creatures die.
A two-drop that grows and ramps every turn.
Value on entry and every attack, and more with an empty hand.
A lord that makes a token with every creature you cast.
Every creature explores. Card and land advantage in one.
Two 3/3s for four mana, and every later token becomes a 3/3.
Will Riker, First in the Field
Two temporary lands every turn: extra mana and two landfall triggers.
